Indigent

IN-di-juhnt · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indigent is poor, poverty-stricken, or needy.

After the factory closed, entire blocks of the mill town slid into indigent poverty within a single year.

Worked Example

The lawyer took the case for free, as she often did for indigent clients who could never otherwise afford legal representation.

Someone with essentially no money to cover life's most basic needs, like legal help, is exactly what indigent describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

destitute: Destitute is the far end of poverty: someone destitute has been stripped of everything -- money, home, and possessions -- with nothing left to fall back on. An indigent person is also seriously poor, but may still hold a small wage or keep a roof; the money simply never covers basic needs.

impoverished: Impoverished means made poor -- the word points at a fall, at something that took the money away: a drought impoverished the farmers, a war impoverished the region. Indigent describes the poverty itself, however it arrived: an indigent person cannot cover life's most basic needs.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

affluent: having a great deal of money

prosperous: financially successful and thriving

Where it sits · how deep the poverty runs — struggling → indigent → penniless

struggling vs. indigent: Struggling is milder than indigent: a struggling family has trouble paying its bills, while an indigent one is deeper in poverty, unable to afford even basic needs.

penniless vs. indigent: Penniless is more extreme than indigent: an indigent person lives in serious poverty, but a penniless one has gone further still, with literally no money at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — indig

Root — indig: to need, to lack (from Latin indigere, 'to need,' built from indu- 'in' + egere 'to need')

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: having the quality of (Latin -ens)

Put it together

Put it together: Indigent comes from indig ('to need, to lack,' from Latin indigere -- itself built from indu- 'in' plus egere 'to need') + -ent. Someone indigent is, at the root, a person genuinely lacking what they need.

Use the root in a new word: indigence

Use the root in a new word: indigence: The charity's annual report described a sharp rise in indigence across the region since the factory closed.

Root Check

Word Choice

Indigent describes a person's poverty directly. It connects naturally to pittance (earlier in this unit): being paid a pittance for long enough is one common path into becoming indigent.
